examples: She is *an autodidact* who taught herself three languages. (a/an: saying what somebody is)
He is writing *a thesis* on climate education. (a/an: first mention)
The professor posted *the syllabus* online yesterday. (the: known to both speakers)
*The curriculum* was redesigned after the new law passed. (the: the only one)
Dr. Lane is *the most erudite* scholar in the department. (the + superlative)
*Plagiarism* is treated as a serious offense here. (no article: general)
*The plagiarism* in his paper was discovered by software. (the: specific)
*Pedagogy* keeps evolving with new technology. (no article: abstract, general)
*The pedagogy* of that school favors group projects. (the: specific)
She invented *a mnemonic* to remember every date. (a/an: first mention)
He passed thanks to *a* desperate *cram* the night before. (a/an: singular countable)
She bounced back quickly after *the flunk* in chemistry. (the: specific known event)
grammar.explanation:
Use **a / an** with a singular countable noun when you say what something is or mention it for the first time. Words like *autodidact*, *thesis*, or *mnemonic* follow this pattern: first *a thesis*, then *the thesis*.

Switch to **the** once the thing is known to both speakers, usually because you already mentioned it. So *a syllabus* on first mention becomes *the syllabus* afterwards.

**The** also marks the only one of its kind and goes before superlatives. Think of *the curriculum* of one school system, or *the most erudite* professor on the staff.

Use **no article** for general ideas with plural or uncountable nouns. *Plagiarism is dishonest* is general, but *the plagiarism in her thesis* points to one specific case.

At C1 level, watch abstract nouns carefully: *pedagogy* in general takes no article, yet *the pedagogy of this college* is specific and needs **the**. Generic versus specific is the real test.

General habits and repeated actions also take no article, even with verbs like *cram* or *flunk*. Compare *students cram before exams* in general with *the students who flunked yesterday* as one known group.

Some fixed expressions never take an article: *at home*, *to work*, *at school*, meals like *lunch*, days and months, and *next / last* plus a time word. And **the** appears with familiar town places, such as *the library* or *the cinema*.
